The first thing the new night janitor noticed was that someone had been watering the plastic plant.

There was a dark ring on the carpet beneath it. The leaves shone with the particular confidence of objects that had never needed anything.

He put a folded rag under the pot and went on cleaning.

The building had twelve floors, most of them occupied by people who spent their days explaining things to people on other floors. At night, their explanations remained on whiteboards.

*Who owns this?*

*What does success look like?*

*Circle back.*

He cleaned around the questions.

On Thursday, he found a paper cup beside the plant, half full of water. On Friday, the rag was soaked again.

He considered leaving a note. **PLASTIC**, perhaps. But there was something unpleasant about the word in capital letters. It seemed liable to describe more than the plant.

Instead, he bought a small pothos from the grocery store.

He tucked it into the big pot, between the artificial stems, where its five imperfect leaves were almost invisible. Then he went upstairs to deal with a coffee spill that had passed through three layers of paperwork.

For several weeks, nothing happened that anyone would put in a report.

The water kept coming.

The pothos made a sixth leaf.

By winter, a green runner had slipped over the lip of the pot. Someone turned it toward the window. Someone else brought a saucer. A yellow sticky note appeared on the wall:

*Does anybody know what kind this is?*

Underneath, in different handwriting:

*Pothos. Let the soil dry out a little between waterings.*

The janitor took away the rag.

In March, he finally met the person with the paper cup: a young man from the seventh floor, standing over the pot with a doubtful expression.

“I think I overdid it at first,” the young man said.

“A little.”

“My mother has plants. I never paid attention.”

The janitor leaned his mop against the wall. He showed him how to press a finger into the soil.

A few months later, when the offices moved to another building, the plant went with them. Two people carried it into the elevator, arguing gently about whether the van would be too cold.

Behind it, on the carpet, was a pale circle surrounded by the wear of passing shoes.

The janitor vacuumed the empty space. Then he unplugged the machine and wound the cord carefully around its hooks.
